# Introduction to Daniel

## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of the book of Daniel

1. Daniel and his friends resolve not to defile themselves (1:1–21)
2. Daniel interprets Nebuchadnezzar’s dream about a statue (2:1–49)
3. God delivers Daniel’s friends from the fiery furnace (3:1–30)
4. Daniel interprets Nebuchadnezzar’s dream about a tree (4:1–37)
5. Daniel interprets the writing on the wall at Belshazzar’s feast (5:1–31)
6. God keeps Daniel safe in the den of lions (6:1–28)
7. Daniel’s vision of four beasts (7:1–28)
8. Daniel’s vision of a ram and a goat (8:1–27)
9. Daniel’s prayer for the restoration of Jerusalem and Gabriel’s explanation (9:1–27)
10. Daniel’s vision of an angel and the kings of the north and south (10:1–12:13)
    1. Daniel has a vision and a man appears to him to explain it (10:1–11:1)
    2. The wars between the kings of the south and north (11:2–45)
    3. What will happen at “the time of the end” (12:1–13)

### What is the Book of Daniel about?

The first part of the book of Daniel (chapters 1–6) relates stories about four young men whom the Babylonians took from the kingdom of Judah as prisoners. One of these men was named Daniel. He had three friends, to whom the Babylonians gave the names Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. These stories tell how these young men were faithful to God while living in a pagan land and serving a pagan king. They tell how God protected them and rewarded them because they were faithful. They also tell how God gave Daniel the ability to interpret dreams and explain mysteries.

The second part of the book of Daniel (chapters 7–12) relates several prophetic visions that Daniel had. These chapters also describe, in several cases, the glorious appearance of angelic messengers who explained to Daniel what his visions meant.

### What title should translators use for this book?

Translators can use the traditional title “The book of Daniel” or just “Daniel.” They might also call this book “Stories and Visions of Daniel” or “What Daniel Did and What God Showed Him.”

### Who wrote the Book of Daniel?

The first six chapters of the book speak of Daniel and his friends in the third person (as “he” and “they”). This suggests that someone else, perhaps another Judean who was exiled in Babylon with them, may have written these chapters to record how they remained faithful to God and how God protected them.

In the last six chapters of the book, Daniel speaks of himself in the first person (saying “I, Daniel”). (The seventh chapter serves as a transition; it begins by speaking of Daniel in the third person, but this introduces an account by Daniel himself that ends with this first-person attestation.) This indicates that Daniel himself wrote this part of the book.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

## Part 3: Important Translation Issues

### The meaning of Daniel’s visions

Even though angelic messengers explain to Daniel what his visions mean, it is not entirely clear to modern readers what historic time periods they predicted or whether they predict things that will happen at the end of the world. It is not necessary to come to conclusions about this in order to translate the book. The language in the visions is straightforward and descriptive, and translation teams should be able to reflect successfully in their languages what it says. What it means is a matter for preachers and teachers of the Scriptures to try to understand and explain.

### The original languages of the book of Daniel

Half of the book of Daniel is written in Hebrew, and the other half of the book is written in Aramaic. These halves do not correspond with the two parts that are stories and visions. Instead, chapters 1 and 8–12 are in Hebrew, while chapters 2–7 are in Aramaic. This means that the first chapter of each part of the book is in a different language from the rest of that part. In the first part, the Hebrew chapter introduces a transition from the young men’s former life in Jerusalem to their life in the Babylonian and Persian courts, where Aramaic was spoken. In the second part, the Aramaic chapter introduces a transition from the affairs of those foreign courts to matters that affect the Jewish people more directly. Daniel and his three friends were native speakers of Hebrew who had to learn Aramaic (1:4), so they or others who were with them would have been able to put together a book like this that used both languages.

Even in the English ULT text, some of the differences between the original Hebrew and Aramaic texts will be evident. For example, translators may already have encountered the common Hebrew expression “answered and said” in their work on other books. In the Aramaic sections of Daniel, the equivalent expression is “answered and was saying.” It is not necessary to try to show such differences in your translation. Consistently say things in the way that is most natural and meaningful in your translation.

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **three**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. In this verse, the number identifies the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim. Alternate translation: [In the third year of the reign]

Here, **hand** represents “power” or “control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the Lord gave into his control]
The word **Ashpenaz** is the name of a man.

The author is speaking as if all the people descended from the man Israel were his **sons**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the people of Israel]

The author is speaking as if the members of the royal family were **seed** that the kingdom had produced. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [both from the royal family]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **kingdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [both from the sons of the royal family]

For poetic purposes, the author is using two different words that have basically the same meaning. The ULT translates each one as **knowledge** because English does not have two different words that it can use in this context. But if your language does, it would be appropriate to use them here. Alternate translation: [knowers of knowledge and understanders of information]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.
Here, **tongue** represents “language.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and language of the Chaldeans]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **wisdom** and **knowledge**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [in everything wise and who knew many things and who understood many things]

The author is using **the matter of a day in its day** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a set amount for each day.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a set amount for each day]

Daniel is using this possessive form to mean the food and wine that the king himself eats and drinks. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from the same food that the king eats and the same wine that he drinks]

The pronoun **them** refers to the three years of the young men’s training, while the pronoun **they** refers to the young men. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and at the end of those three years the young men would serve]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of or in the presence of the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before the king]

The author is introducing **Daniel**, **Hananiah**, **Mishael**, and **Azariah** as new participants in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [four young men whose names were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah]

1.quote: בֵּ֣לְטְשַׁאצַּ֗ר וְ⁠לַֽ⁠חֲנַנְיָה֙ שַׁדְרַ֔ךְ וּ⁠לְ⁠מִֽישָׁאֵ֣ל מֵישַׁ֔ךְ וְ⁠לַ⁠עֲזַרְיָ֖ה עֲבֵ֥ד נְגֽוֹ
1.text: The words **Belteshazzar**, **Shadrach**, **Meshach**, and **Abednego** are the Babylonian names of these young men.

1.quote: וְ⁠לַֽ⁠חֲנַנְיָה֙ שַׁדְרַ֔ךְ וּ⁠לְ⁠מִֽישָׁאֵ֣ל מֵישַׁ֔ךְ וְ⁠לַ⁠עֲזַרְיָ֖ה עֲבֵ֥ד נְגֽוֹ
1.text: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and to Hananiah, he gave the name Shadrach; and to Mishael, he gave the name Meshach; and to Azariah, he gave the name Abednego]

The author is using **set upon his heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “resolved” or “firmly decided.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But Daniel firmly decided]

The author is using **gave Daniel to favor and to compassions** as a common expression of the culture to mean “caused the chief of the eunuchs to regard Daniel with favor and kindness.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And God caused Daniel to be regarded with favor and compassion]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **favor** and **compassions**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [to be regarded favorably and compassionately]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of the chief of the eunuchs. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of] or [in front of]

The chief of the eunuchs is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **fear** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself is afraid of what the king might do to him. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I myself fear my lord the king] or [for my part, I fear]

1.quote: אֲשֶׁ֡ר לָ⁠מָּה֩ יִרְאֶ֨ה אֶת־פְּנֵי⁠כֶ֜ם זֹֽעֲפִ֗ים מִן־הַ⁠יְלָדִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר כְּ⁠גִֽילְ⁠כֶ֔ם
1.text: The chief of the eunuchs is using the question form to express his fear of what the king might do to him if the young men looked unhealthy. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [For I am afraid that he will see your faces looking worse than your peers!]

The chief of the eunuchs is using **endanger my head with the king** as a common expression of the culture to mean “cause the king to have me executed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then you would cause the king to have me beheaded]

1.quote: אֲשֶׁ֡ר לָ⁠מָּה֩ יִרְאֶ֨ה אֶת־פְּנֵי⁠כֶ֜ם זֹֽעֲפִ֗ים מִן־הַ⁠יְלָדִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר כְּ⁠גִֽילְ⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠חִיַּבְתֶּ֥ם אֶת־רֹאשִׁ֖⁠י לַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ
1.text: The word **you** is plural here because the chief of the eunuchs is addressing Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah together, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

A **steward** is a kind of official who was put in charge of overseeing and caring for others. If your readers would not be familiar with what a steward is, you could use the name of a similar person that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the caretaker] or [the overseer]

Daniel is referring to himself and his companions in the third person as **your servants** to show respect and humility before the steward. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this in the first person. Alternate translation: [us]

Daniel is using the pronoun **them** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and let us be given some vegetables to eat]

Daniel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He means that he wants the steward to give them vegetables to eat and water to drink. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and let them give to us vegetables to eat and water to drink]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **appearances** and **appearance**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Then call us before you to see how we look and how the youths look after they have been]

The expression **it was seen** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [their faces looked]

The author is using **fatter of flesh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “healthier” or “better nourished.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and better nourished]

1.quote: וְ⁠הַ⁠יְלָדִ֤ים הָ⁠אֵ֨לֶּה֙ אַרְבַּעְתָּ֔⁠ם נָתַ֨ן לָ⁠הֶ֧ם הָֽ⁠אֱלֹהִ֛ים
1.text: The author is stating the topic **these four youths** at the beginning of the sentence and then referring back to them with the pronoun **them**. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the four youths together with the information about what God gave to them. Alternate translation: [And God gave these four youths]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of Nebuchadnezzar. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into the presence of Nebuchadnezzar] or [in front of Nebuchadnezzar]

The expression **was found** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he found none]
The pronoun **them** refers to all the young men whom the king had brought before him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from all of the other young men]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **wisdom** and **understanding**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [matter requiring them to be wise and to understand well]

The author is using **ten hands above** as a common expression of the culture to mean “ten times better than.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [ten times better than all of]

The terms **magicians** and **enchanters** describe people who claimed to have secret knowledge and the ability to perform magic and interpret dreams and omens. If your readers would not be familiar with what these people did, you could use the names of similar people that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [the people who practiced magic and claimed secret knowledge]

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **one**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [until the first year that Cyrus was king]

2.text:
# Daniel 2 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Nebuchadnezzar has a troubling dream that he cannot remember (1)
2. His advisors fail to tell him the dream, so he orders their execution (2–13)
3. Daniel appeals for time, and God shows him the dream (14–19)
4. Daniel praises God (20–23)
5. Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar his dream and its meaning (24–45)
6. Nebuchadnezzar rewards Daniel and his friends (46–49)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in Daniel’s prayer of thanksgiving in [2:20–23](../02/20.md).

The expression **year of two** uses a cardinal number where your language might use an ordinal number, since it refers to the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar. If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **two**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [In the second year]

Daniel is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [Nebuchadnezzar dreamed]

The expression **his spirit was troubled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And this troubled his spirit]

Daniel is using **his sleep finished for him** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Nebuchadnezzar was unable to sleep. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he could not sleep]

The terms **magicians**, **enchanters**, and **sorcerers** are different kinds of people who were thought to have special knowledge or powers, such as interpreting dreams, using magic, or communicating with spirits. If your readers would not be familiar with what these are, you could use the names of similar people that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [the users of magic and the spell-casters and the fortune-tellers]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in the presence of the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of the king]

Nebuchadnezzar is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [I dreamed]

The expression **is troubled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and it troubles my spirit]

The Chaldeans are using **live forever** as a common expression of the culture to mean “may you live for a long time.” It was a respectful way to greet a king. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may you live for a long time]

The Chaldeans are speaking of themselves in the third person as **your servants** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [to us, your humble servants]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and we will interpret it for you]

The expression **and was saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this expression explicitly, here and in its many other occurrences in this book.

The king is using **The word from me is firm** as a common expression of the culture to mean “my decision is final.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My decision is final]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and interpret it for me]

The expression **you will be made** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will have your limbs cut off]

The expression **your houses will be made a rubbish heap** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will turn your houses into a rubbish heap]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and interpret it for me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of honor, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will honor you very much]

Even though the Chaldeans are addressing the king directly, they are speaking of him in the third person as **the king** and of themselves in the third person as **his servants** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form using the second person and the first person. Alternate translation: [O king, please tell us your servants the dream]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and we will interpret it for you]

See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to the book of Daniel. In this context, the king is using it to indicate that what follows is the reason for what precedes. Alternate translation: [because]

The king is using **you are buying time** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you are trying to gain more time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are trying extend the time allotted]

The king is using **your decree is one** as a common expression of the culture to mean “there is only one verdict for you all.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [there is only one verdict for you all]

The expression **the time is changed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [circumstances change]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you interpret it correctly]

The Chaldeans are not referring to a specific **man**. They mean people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone]

See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to the book of Daniel. In this context, the wise men are using it to indicate that what follows shows why what precedes is true. Alternate translation: [you may be sure of this because] or [after all,]

The Chaldeans are using **flesh** to represent human beings, who are mortal. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]

See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to the book of Daniel. In this context, the author is using it to indicate that follows is the result of what he has just described. Alternate translation: [Because of this] or [As a result]

The terms **became angry** and **became very furious** mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [became extremely angry]

The expression **the wise men were to be killed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that people should kill the wise men]

The expression **to be killed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And they sought Daniel and his friends in order to kill them]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **prudence** and **discretion**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [prudently and discreetly]
The word **Arioch** is the name of a man.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he might explain to the king what the dream meant]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mercies**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that they might seek to be treated mercifully]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mystery**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what was hidden] or [what they did not know]

The expression **the mystery was revealed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God revealed the mystery to Daniel]

David is saying what he wants to happen. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about this form of speech, and follow the decision you have made as a team about how speakers will express in such contexts what they want to happen. Alternate translation: [I desire for God’s name to be blessed]

The expression **be blessed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May people bless the name of God]
Daniel is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. Alternate translation: [May God be blessed]

“His name, of God” is a doubling of reference. The phrase names God twice, once by pronoun, “name,” and once explicitly as “God.” It might seem that the expression **his name, of God** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [May God be blessed]
Here, **his name** represents God himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [God himself]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **wisdom** and **power**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [being wise and being mighty]

Daniel is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, **from eternity** and **to eternity**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for all time]

2.quote: יָהֵ֤ב חָכְמְתָ⁠א֙ לְ⁠חַכִּימִ֔ין וּ⁠מַנְדְּעָ֖⁠א לְ⁠יָדְעֵ֥י בִינָֽה
2.text: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [the one giving wisdom and understanding to those who are wise]

Daniel is using the adjective **wise** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to wise people] or [to those who are wise]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **knowledge** and **understanding**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and enabling those who can discern to know things]

2.quote: יָהֵ֤ב חָכְמְתָ⁠א֙ לְ⁠חַכִּימִ֔ין וּ⁠מַנְדְּעָ֖⁠א לְ⁠יָדְעֵ֥י בִינָֽה
2.text: This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

Daniel is using the plural adjectives **the deep** and **the hidden** as nouns to mean certain kinds of things. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [deep things and hidden things]

The terms **the deep** and **the hidden** mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [things that are very difficult to know] or [things that are very obscure]

2.quote: יָדַע֙ מָ֣ה בַ⁠חֲשׁוֹכָ֔⁠א ו⁠נהיר⁠א עִמֵּ֥⁠הּ שְׁרֵֽא
2.text: Daniel is speaking of hidden things as if they were **darkness** and of what God knows as if it were **light**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he knows what is secret, and understanding resides with him]

# Daniel 3 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Nebuchadnezzar orders his officials to worship his golden statue (1–7)
2. Officials report Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego for not worshiping (8–12)
3. Nebuchadnezzar threatens them, but they refuse (13–18)
4. Nebuchadnezzar has them thrown into a very hot furnace (19–23)
5. God sends an angel to rescue them (24–27)
6. Nebuchadnezzar honors God and promotes them (28–30)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did Nebuchadnezzar make a statue covered completely with gold?

When Daniel interprets Nebuchadnezzar’s dream in chapter 2, he explains that the parts of the statue in his dream that were made of different metals represented different empires. Nebuchadnezzar’s Babylonian empire was the head of gold. The dream, which Daniel said God gave Nebuchadnezzar to show him what would happen in the future, indicated that this empire would end and others would succeed it. By building a great statue like the one in his dream but covering it all in gold, Nebuchadnezzar was asserting instead that his empire would never end. Bowing down to the statue was an act of agreeing with him and disagreeing with what God had said in the dream. In many places, the law of Moses already forbade Israelites to bow down to any idols (for example, in the Ten Commandments in [Exodus 20:4–5](../exo/20/04.md)). But this was a further reason why these Judean young men had to refuse to worship the statue even if they were executed as a result.

### Why does this chapter not describe Daniel refusing to worship the statue?

This chapter only describes Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refusing to worship Nebuchadnezzar’s golden statue. However, readers should not infer from this that Daniel did worship it. The last verse of the previous chapter, which provides a transition into this chapter, says that Nebuchadnezzar “appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the work of the province of Babylon. But Daniel was at the gate of the king.” In other words, Daniel remained at the royal court, while his three friends had responsibilities out in the province of Babylon, and that is where Nebuchadnezzar set up his statue (3:1). So Daniel was not among the provincial officials who were summoned to the dedication of the statue. His actions in the rest of the book (for example, in chapter 6, where he continues to pray to God even though he would be executed for doing this) show that if he had been summoned, he too would have refused to worship the statue.

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter consists of a letter that King Nebuchadnezzar wrote to all the subjects in his empire. In this letter, he relates an experience he had that taught him that God, whom he calls “the Most High” and “the king of the heavens,” determines what people will reign over earthly kingdoms and for how long.

1. The greeting at the start of the letter (1–3)
2. Nebuchadnezzar has a dream and asks Daniel to interpret it (4–18)
3. Daniel explains the meaning of the dream (19–27)
4. What the dream depicted happens to Nebuchadnezzar (28–36)
5. The closing of the letter (37)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [4:3](../04/03.md) and [4:34–35](../04/34.md).

# Daniel 5 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. At a feast that Belshazzar gives, a hand writes something on the palace wall (1–6)
2. No one else can read the writing, but the queen mother recommends Daniel (7–12)
3. Daniel reads and interprets the writing (13–28)
4. Belshazzar rewards Daniel, but he is killed that night by the invading Persians (29–30)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did Belshazzar want to drink from vessels from the Jerusalem temple?

Belshazzar and his guests used vessels from the Jerusalem temple to drink toasts in honor of the gods their idols represented. This was most likely a deliberate act repudiating the God of that temple in favor of traditional Babylonian gods. Daniel reminds Belshazzar that he knew all about how his grandfather Nebuchadnezzar had come to honor and worship that God as the true God. But many interpreters suggest that, with the Babylonians now under dire threat from the Persians, Belshazzar believed that if he returned to his traditional gods, they would rescue him and his kingdom. In this culture, when one kingdom conquered another, it would take the idols of the conquered kingdom and put them in the temple of one of its own gods as trophies of victory. There were no idols representing Yahweh, so the Babylonians took the vessels from his temple instead. It appears that Nebuchadnezzar had kept these in a temple and not used them for common purposes. Belshazzar, by using them at a banquet to drink toasts to false gods, was defiling them. That is why he came under such serious and immediate judgment.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Mene, Mene, Tekel, and Parsin

No one could read what the writing on the wall said, so it is probable that it was written in some language and script other than the Aramaic that was spoken in Babylon. God enabled Daniel to understand what the writing was saying, and he translated it into Aramaic words. The meaning of these words is evident from what Daniel says about them: “mene” means to “number,” “tekel” means to “weigh,” and “peres” means to “divide.” (The term “mene” is probably repeated for emphasis, to show the certainty of God’s judgment against Belshazzar. “Parsin” in verse 25 is the plural of “peres” in verse 28.) The ULT and UST texts write these Aramaic words with English letters, spelling them the way they sound in English. Translators are encouraged to write these words with the letters of their own alphabets and to spell them the way they sound in their own languages.
The word **Belshazzar** is the name of a man.

Daniel is using the adjective **thousand** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a thousand of them]

5.quote: בֵּלְשַׁאצַּ֣ר מַלְכָּ֗⁠א עֲבַד֙ לְחֶ֣ם רַ֔ב לְ⁠רַבְרְבָנ֖וֹ⁠הִי אֲלַ֑ף
5.text: Belshazzar is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He means that he made a feast for a thousand of his nobles. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [King Belshazzar made a great feast for a thousand of his nobles]

Daniel is using the phrase **in the taste of the wine** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Belshazzar was under the influence of the wine that he had been drinking. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Belshazzar became drunk and said] or [while under the influence of the wine]

Elsewhere in Daniel and Ezra, in the Aramaic portions of Scripture, the term that the ULT translates here as **taste** means “command” or “decree.” While many interpreters favor “taste” here, the sense of “command” would also suit the context and have the same basic meaning. Alternate translation: [Belshazzar said by command of the wine]

Belshazzar is using the term **father** to mean “grandfather,” or more generally, “ancestor.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Nebuchadnezzar his grandfather]

5.quote: וְ⁠יִשְׁתּ֣וֹן בְּ⁠ה֗וֹן מַלְכָּ⁠א֙ וְ⁠רַבְרְבָנ֔וֹ⁠הִי שֵׁגְלָתֵ֖⁠הּ וּ⁠לְחֵנָתֵֽ⁠הּ
5.text: Drinking from these **vessels** was a symbolic action by which the king mocked the God whose temple was in Jerusalem. Verse 4 makes clear that the Belshazzar wanted to honor his own idols rather than God, whom his grandfather Nebuchadnezzar had learned to fear and honor. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote.
The pronoun **they** refers to the servants of the king. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Then the king’s servants brought]

Daniel is using the possessive form to describe a **temple** that is characterized by being a **house** for **God**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the temple that was the house of God]

Daniel is using the phrase **his splendors changed** as a common expression of the culture to mean that the king’s face turned pale. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the color drained from his face]

Daniel is using the phrase **the joints of his loins were loosened** as a common expression of the culture to mean that the king suddenly became weak with fear. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And his body became weak with terror]

The expression **were loosened** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [grew weak] or [came loose]

Daniel is using the phrase **his knees knocked, this to this** as a common expression of the culture to mean that the king’s knees struck against each other because he was so afraid. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his knees banged together in fear]

Daniel is using the phrase **The king called out in strength** as a common expression of the culture to mean that the king raised his voice. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The king called out with a loud voice]

The king is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Whoever reads this writing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and shows me what it means]
These were symbols of high rank and authority. Alternate translation: [shall be granted high rank]

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **third**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [and only two others shall rule above him in the kingdom]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [or to tell the king what it meant]

5.quote: מַלְכָּ֤⁠א בֵלְשַׁאצַּר֙ שַׂגִּ֣יא מִתְבָּהַ֔ל וְ⁠זִיוֺ֖⁠הִי שָׁנַ֣יִן עֲל֑וֹ⁠הִי וְ⁠רַבְרְבָנ֖וֹ⁠הִי מִֽשְׁתַּבְּשִֽׁין
5.text: The expressions **was being alarmed** and **were being perplexed** are passive verbal forms. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express these ideas in active form or in another way that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [King Belshazzar felt great alarm, and his splendors were changing upon him, and his nobles felt perplexity]

The implication is that this woman was the queen mother, that is, the mother of the king, since the king’s wives were already present at the feast. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The mother of the king came in]

The queen is using the expression **live to eternities** as a common expression of the culture to express a respectful wish that the king would have a long and prosperous life. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [O king, may you enjoy long life and prosperity]

The expression **may your splendors not be changed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and do not let your face lose its color]

The queen is using the possessive form to describe a **spirit** that is characterized by coming from **the holy gods**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is a spirit that comes from the holy gods]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **light**, **understanding**, and **wisdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [abilities to enlighten and to understand and to be wise]

The queen is speaking as if the ability to understand things were **light**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [insight]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the gods** were thought to have perfect wisdom, so this man had extraordinary **wisdom**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and wisdom as extraordinary as the wisdom that the gods were thought to have]

The expression **were found in him** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [showed themselves in him]

The queen is repeating the information that Nebuchadnezzar was an illustrious predecessor of Belshazzar in order to emphasize the qualifications of Daniel. If your language can repeat information for emphasis, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the emphasis. Alternate translation: [And your grandfather, King Nebuchadnezzar, that great emperor]

Here, the phrase **all before that** introduces the reason why the queen says the king should summon Daniel, namely that Daniel has these exceptional abilities. Use a natural way in your language for introducing a reason.

Here the queen is speaking as if solving difficult problems were **loosening of knots**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [untangling difficult problems] or [solving difficult problems]
The word **Belteshazzar** is the Babylonian name of Daniel.

The queen is using the term **Now** to focus her listeners’ attention on what she is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [So]

The expression **let Daniel be called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [have someone call Daniel]

The expression **Then Daniel was brought in** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Then they brought Daniel in]

The king is using the phrase **the sons of the captivity of Judah** as a common expression of the culture to refer to the people who had been taken away from Judah as captives. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the Judean captives whom]

5.quote: אנתה־ה֤וּא דָנִיֵּאל֙ דִּֽי־מִן־בְּנֵ֤י גָלוּתָ⁠א֙ דִּ֣י יְה֔וּד דִּ֥י הַיְתִ֛י מַלְכָּ֥⁠א אַ֖בִ⁠י מִן־יְהֽוּד
5.text: The king is using the question form to express his certainty about Daniel’s identity, not to request information. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [So you are Daniel, who is from the sons of the captivity of Judah that my father the king brought from Judah!]

Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The expression **are found in you** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [belong to you]

Belshazzar is using the term **And now** to focus Daniel’s attention on what he is about to say. The king introduces a major point and then his main point. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [So]

The expression **have been brought in before me** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [my servants have brought in before me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how to interpret]

Again, Belshazzar is using the term **And now** to focus Daniel’s attention on what he is about to say. This time he will deliver his main point. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [And so]

Belshazzar is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I have heard** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that, unlike his wise men who were not able to interpret the writing, he himself has heard that Daniel is able to interpret it. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But I myself have heard]

The king is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root: **interpret interpretations**. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [give interpretations of difficult things]

Belshazzar is speaking as if difficult problems were **knots** that needed to be loosened. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [untangle complicated problems] or [solve extremely difficult problems]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and interpret it]

Wearing purple clothing and a gold chain around one’s neck was a symbolic action by which the king showed that Daniel would receive great honor and authority. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I will honor you by having you wear purple and by putting a chain of gold around your neck]

5.quote: מַתְּנָתָ⁠ךְ֙ לָ֣⁠ךְ לֶֽהֶוְיָ֔ן וּ⁠נְבָ֥זְבְּיָתָ֖⁠ךְ לְ⁠אָחֳרָ֣ן הַ֑ב
5.text: Daniel is saying what he wants the king to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [You may keep your gifts for yourself, and I want you to give your rewards to another]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [make him know what it means]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **greatness**, **honor**, and **majesty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the kingdom and everything that made him great and honored and majestic]

Here, **languages** represents the people who speak those languages. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [peoples, nations, and speakers of every language]

The terms **trembling** and **fearing** mean similar things. Daniel is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [extremely afraid]

5.quote: דִּֽי־הֲוָ֨ה צָבֵ֜א הֲוָ֣א קָטֵ֗ל וְ⁠דִֽי־הֲוָ֤ה צָבֵא֙ הֲוָ֣ה מַחֵ֔א וְ⁠דִֽי־הֲוָ֤ה צָבֵא֙ הֲוָ֣ה מָרִ֔ים וְ⁠דִֽי־הֲוָ֥ה צָבֵ֖א הֲוָ֥ה מַשְׁפִּֽיל
5.text: Daniel is referring to Nebuchadnezzar’s complete power over everyone by naming opposite actions: whom **he was killing** and whom **he was letting live**, and whom **he was lifting up** and whom **he was humbling**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [He had complete power over everyone, deciding whether they lived or died and whether they became important or unimportant]

Daniel is speaking of Nebuchadnezzar becoming proud and arrogant as if **his heart lifted** itself **up and his spirit became strong to be proud**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he became very proud and stubbornly arrogant]

The expression **he was brought down** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God brought him down]

Here, **the throne of his kingdom** represents his royal power and authority as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his royal authority as king]

Here, Daniel uses the pronoun **they** in an impersonal sense to indicate that God removed Nebuchadnezzar’s glory. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and God removed his glory]

The expression **he was driven** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God drove him]

5.quote: וּ⁠מִן־בְּנֵי֩ אֲנָשָׁ֨⁠א טְרִ֜יד וְ⁠לִבְבֵ֣⁠הּ ׀ עִם־חֵיוְתָ֣⁠א שוי וְ⁠עִם־עֲרָֽדַיָּ⁠א֙ מְדוֹרֵ֔⁠הּ עִשְׂבָּ֤⁠א כְ⁠תוֹרִין֙ יְטַ֣עֲמוּנֵּ֔⁠הּ וּ⁠מִ⁠טַּ֥ל שְׁמַיָּ֖⁠א גִּשְׁמֵ֣⁠הּ יִצְטַבַּ֑ע עַ֣ד דִּֽי־יְדַ֗ע דִּֽי־שַׁלִּ֞יט אֱלָהָ֤⁠א עלי⁠א בְּ⁠מַלְכ֣וּת אֲנָשָׁ֔⁠א וּ⁠לְ⁠מַן־דִּ֥י יִצְבֵּ֖ה יְהָקֵ֥ים עלי⁠ה
5.text: The pronoun **he** refers to Nebuchadnezzar, while the pronoun **he** in **whom that he wishes, he sets up over it** refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Nebuchadnezzar was driven from the sons of man and his heart resembled with an animal and his dwelling was with the wild donkeys. They fed him grass like oxen and his body was wet with the dew of the heavens until Nebuchadnezzar knew that the Most High God is ruler over the kingdom of man and whomever God wishes, God sets up over it]

Daniel is using the phrase **the sons of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean human beings in general. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [humanity]

The point of this comparison is that just as an **animal** thinks and acts without human reason, so Nebuchadnezzar’s **heart**, or mind, became like that. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and his mind lost human reason and became like that of an animal]

The point of this comparison is that just as **oxen** eat grass, so Nebuchadnezzar was fed **grass** to eat. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They fed him grass to eat, just as oxen eat grass]

Daniel uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between what Belshazzar knew about Nebuchadnezzar and his own failure to humble himself. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Nonetheless, you]

Daniel is speaking of Belshazzar’s refusal to become humble as if he could physically lower his own **heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [have not become humble]

Daniel is using **all before that** as a common expression of the culture to mean “although.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [even though] or [despite the fact that]

Daniel is speaking of Belshazzar’s arrogance toward God as if he had physically **lifted** himself **up against the Lord of the heavens**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But you have acted arrogantly toward the Lord of the heavens]

The expression **have been brought** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they have brought]

Here, **your breath** represents your life, and being **in his hand** represents being under his control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your life is under his control]

Daniel is speaking of everything Belshazzar does as if his actions were **ways**, or paths, that belong to God. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and everything that you do he determines]

The expression **was sent** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [came]

The expression **was inscribed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [appeared]

The words **Mene**, **Mene**, **Tekel**, and **Parsin** are words in the original language. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their original form or if you will instead translate their meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the original words, you could spell them the way they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [‘Numbered,’ ‘Numbered,’ ‘Weighed,’ ‘Divided.’]

Daniel is speaking of God judging Belshazzar as if God had **weighed** him **on the scales and found** him **deficient**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God has examined you and determined that you do not meet his standard]

The expression **you have been weighed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God weighed you]

The expression **found deficient** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he has found you deficient]

The implication is that God is the one who has divided the kingdom and that the Medes and the Persians will take control of it, which happened soon afterward. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [God has divided your kingdom and has given it to the Medes and the Persians, who will soon rule over it]

The expression **has been divided** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [has broken apart] or [God has divided]

The expression **given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God has given it]

In this verse, the word **Mede** is singular in form, but it refers to all of the Medes as a group, and the word **Persian** refers to all of the Persians as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “Mede” and “Persian.” Alternate translation: [to the Medes and the Persians]
Here, the pronoun **they** refers to the servants of Belshazzar. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and his servants clothed Daniel]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **proclamation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and they had it announced]

The expression **was killed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [met his death]

Daniel is using the phrase **a son of 62 years** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Darius was 62 years old. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when he was 62 years old]

6.text:
# Daniel 6 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. King Darius appoints high officials and wants Daniel to be the highest (1–3)
2. The other officials get Darius to make a law forbidding prayer (4–9)
3. Daniel continues to pray to God, and the officials insist that Darius punish him (10–16)
4. Daniel is thrown into a den of lions, but God protects him (16–23)
5. The other officials are thrown into the den and killed, and Darius honors God (24–28)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [6:26–27](../06/26.md).

The author is using **It seemed good before Darius** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Darius decided this.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Darius thought it best]

**Satraps** were provincial governors in the ancient Persian empire, each of whom ruled one region on behalf of the king. If your readers would not be familiar with what satraps were, you could use the name of a similar kind of official that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [provincial governors]

**Sareks** were high officials who supervised the satraps in the ancient Persian empire. If your readers would not be familiar with what sareks were, you could use the name of a similar kind of official that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [three chief administrators]

The expression **all before that** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because]

Here, **an excellent spirit** represents “exceptional character and ability.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he had outstanding character and ability]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **occasion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to find some way to accuse Daniel]

Daniel is using **all before that** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because]

The expression **was not found in him** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they did not find in him]
Here, the word **that** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

6.quote: לָ֧א נְהַשְׁכַּ֛ח לְ⁠דָנִיֵּ֥אל דְּנָ֖ה כָּל־עִלָּ֑א לָהֵ֕ן הַשְׁכַּ֥חְנָֽה עֲל֖וֹ⁠הִי
6.text: If it would appear in your language that these men were making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [The only occasion we will find against this Daniel will be something]

The officials are using **live to eternities** as a common expression of the culture to mean “may you live a very long time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may you live long]

The officials are using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root, **petitions a petition**. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

The expression **shall be thrown into a den of lions** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [is someone whom your servants shall throw into a den of lions]

The officials are using **which does not pass away** as a common expression of the culture to mean “which cannot be revoked.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [which is without end]

Daniel is using **All before this** as a common expression of the culture to mean “so” or “therefore.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [So then] or [Therefore]

The expression **the writing had been signed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the king had signed the writing]

6.quote: וְ⁠כַוִּ֨ין פְּתִיחָ֥ן לֵ⁠הּ֙ בְּ⁠עִלִּיתֵ֔⁠הּ נֶ֖גֶד יְרוּשְׁלֶ֑ם
6.text: Here the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Daniel is using **all before that** as a common expression of the culture to mean “just as.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [just as] or [in the same way as]

6.quote: הֲ⁠לָ֧א אֱסָ֣ר רְשַׁ֗מְתָּ דִּ֣י כָל־אֱנָ֡שׁ דִּֽי־יִבְעֵה֩ מִן־כָּל־אֱלָ֨הּ וֶֽ⁠אֱנָ֜שׁ עַד & תְּלָתִ֗ין & מִנָּ֣⁠ךְ מַלְכָּ֔⁠א יִתְרְמֵ֕א לְ⁠ג֖וֹב אַרְיָותָ֑⁠א
6.text: The men are using the question form to remind the king of a decree he already made, implying that he must enforce it. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You signed a decree that any man who petitions from any god or man for thirty days, except from you, O king, shall be thrown into a den of lions!]

The expression **shall be thrown into a den of lions** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language.

The officials are using **the sons of the captivity of Judah** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the people who were taken away from Judah as captives.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people who were taken away from Judah as captives]

The officials are using **does not set regard on you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “pays no attention to you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [does not respect you] or [does not obey you]

The author is using **he set his heart on Daniel to deliver him** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the king was determined to rescue Daniel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he resolved to rescue Daniel]

6.quote: בֵּ⁠אדַ֜יִן מַלְכָּ֣⁠א אֲמַ֗ר וְ⁠הַיְתִיו֙ לְ⁠דָ֣נִיֵּ֔אל וּ⁠רְמ֕וֹ לְ⁠גֻבָּ֖⁠א דִּ֣י אַרְיָוָתָ֑⁠א עָנֵ֤ה מַלְכָּ⁠א֙ וְ⁠אָמַ֣ר לְ⁠דָנִיֵּ֔אל אֱלָהָ֗⁠ךְ דִּ֣י אנתה פָּֽלַֽח־לֵ⁠הּ֙ בִּ⁠תְדִירָ֔⁠א ה֖וּא יְשֵׁיזְבִנָּֽ⁠ךְ
6.text: You could put the information about the king speaking to Daniel before the information that they threw Daniel into the den of lions. The UST models one way to do that.

It might seem that the expression **whom you are serving him** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [whom you are serving]

6.quote: וְ⁠הֵיתָ֨יִת֙ אֶ֣בֶן חֲדָ֔ה וְ⁠שֻׂמַ֖ת עַל־פֻּ֣ם גֻּבָּ֑⁠א
6.text: The expression **a stone was brought and set over the mouth of the den** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And servants brought a stone and set it over the mouth of the den]

The author is speaking of **his sleep** as if it were a living thing that could depart from the king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he was unable to sleep]

Daniel is using **live to eternities** as a common expression of the culture to mean “may you live a very long time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [may you live long]

The expression **innocence was found to me before him** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he found me to be innocent]

Daniel is using **all before that** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because]

The expression **Daniel was brought up from the den** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the king’s servants brought Daniel up from the den]

The expression **any harm was not found in him** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they found no harm in him]

The author is using **who had eaten the pieces of Daniel** as a common expression of the culture to mean “who had maliciously accused Daniel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who had maliciously accused Daniel]

6.quote: כְּ֠תַב לְֽ⁠כָל־עַֽמְמַיָּ֞⁠א אֻמַיָּ֧⁠א וְ⁠לִשָּׁנַיָּ֛⁠א דִּֽי־דארין בְּ⁠כָל־אַרְעָ֖⁠א שְׁלָמְ⁠כ֥וֹן יִשְׂגֵּֽא
6.text: The quotation of the letter from King Darius may begin with **to all of the peoples** rather than with **May your peace abound**. (Compare the start of the letter from King Nebuchadnezzar in 4:1.) Alternate translation: [wrote, “To all of the peoples, nations, and languages that are dwelling in all of the earth, may your peace abound”]

Here, **languages** represents “the people who speak those languages.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and speakers of different languages]

The author says **in all of the earth** as an extreme statement for emphasis. The people addressed lived throughout the king’s empire. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [throughout the entire empire]

The king is using **May your peace abound** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I wish you great well-being.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May you prosper greatly]

The expression **From before me a decree is set** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I am making this decree]

The terms **trembling** and **fearing** mean similar things. The king is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [deeply afraid]

The king is using **enduring to eternities** as a common expression of the culture to mean “existing forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he exists forever]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and his kingdom and his rule will never come to an end]

The expression **will not be destroyed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no power can destroy]

The terms **delivering** and **rescuing** mean similar things. The king is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [powerfully saving people]

The terms **signs** and **wonders** mean similar things. The king is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [amazing miracles]

The king is referring to all of creation by naming two major components, **the heavens** and **the earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everywhere in creation]
Here, **hand** represents “power” or “control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the power of the lions]

7.text:
# Daniel 7 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Narrative introduction: Daniel has a dream about four beasts (1)
2. Daniel describes his dream (2–15)
3. Daniel tells how a character in the dream explained its meaning to him (16–27)
4. Daniel concludes this account personally (28)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [7:9–10](../07/09.md) and [7:13–14](../07/13.md).

## Translation issues in this chapter

### Should translations try to identify what the beasts in this dream represent?

The character in the dream who explains its meaning to Daniel tells him, “These great beasts, which are four, are four kings arising from the earth” (7:17). Interpreters have certain understandings of what kingdoms these beasts represent, for example, that the lion represents the Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar, that the bear represents the empire of the Medes and Persians, and so forth. However, we recommend that you do not put anything in the text of your translation or even in a footnote tentatively identifying these kingdoms. Their identity is not certain, and moreover it is not the task of translators to interpret the text, only to represent what it says accurately in their own languages. We recommend similarly that you not offer interpretations of the symbols in chapters 8–12. See the discussion in the introduction to the book of Daniel, “The meaning of Daniel’s visions.”

Daniel is using the time reference **In the year of one to Belshazzar, the king of Babylon** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

In the original language, the number here is a cardinal number, **one**, that has the sense of an ordinal number, “first.” If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **one**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [In the first year of the reign of Belshazzar]
The word **Belshazzar** is the name of a man.

7.quote: דָּנִיֵּאל֙ חֵ֣לֶם חֲזָ֔ה וְ⁠חֶזְוֵ֥י רֵאשֵׁ֖⁠הּ עַֽל־מִשְׁכְּבֵ֑⁠הּ בֵּ⁠אדַ֨יִן֙ חֶלְמָ֣⁠א כְתַ֔ב רֵ֥אשׁ מִלִּ֖ין אֲמַֽר
7.text: Even though Daniel is the one who is reporting this vision, he is speaking of himself in the third person as **Daniel**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I saw a dream and visions of my head upon my bed.
